definition: Defamatory means harming someone's reputation with false statements.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word defamatory. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know defamatory should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The historian sued over the documentary's defamatory claim that he had invented his interview tapes.
An unflattering profile is far milder than a defamatory one: it shows your bad side and stays within its rights, because every word of it may be true.
An insulting remark is offensive to your face and may still be honest; defamatory goes further — false, public, and aimed at what the whole world thinks of you.

Slanderous is defamatory harm in spoken form — the false accusation said aloud, at a meeting or over a phone line. Defamatory is the umbrella term for a reputation-wrecking falsehood in any medium; slanderous commits to speech and speech alone.

Libelous is defamatory harm in fixed form — print, posts, broadcast — the falsehood you can file away and read back. Where defamatory covers a reputation-damaging lie however it travels, libelous commits to the written or recorded version of it.

Defamatory means harming someone's reputation with false statements.
Mid-season, a nameless fan site posted that the goalkeeper had bet against her own club.
No bookmaker, regulator, or teammate ever backed the story, but the transfer offer she had been weighing vanished within the week.
When the club's lawyers called the post defamatory, they meant something precise: a published falsehood that had cost her the one thing a career runs on — her name.
Defamatory is the exact word because it needs both parts: the claim must be false, and it must wound a reputation.
A true exposé can end a career and defame no one; an insult — 'a mediocre keeper' — bruises feelings but states an opinion.
The defamatory statement pretends to be fact, gets the fact wrong, and leaves the damage standing.
Defamatory is the courtroom's word: it accuses a statement of being false and of damaging someone's standing, and both halves must hold.
Its unit-mate scurrilous judges style, not truth — a scurrilous attack is coarse and abusive whether or not a word of it is false, while a defamatory one can be phrased as politely as a legal brief.

Okafor ran the Riverside Chess Club without a whisper of complaint — until the flyer appeared.
Taped to the community-center door, it claimed he had thrown tournament matches for cash, and by Friday the same words were being repeated aloud at the bake sale.
The club's own records told another story: he had won the disputed games, and no money had ever changed hands.
But records travel slower than flyers.
Two families quit the club, and the hardware store quietly dropped its sponsorship.
When the club's secretary finally traced the flyer to a rival organizer, the lawyer's letter called it what it was: defamatory — a fabricated charge that had cost a blameless man his standing.
